doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Concert-pianist ambition, Juilliard and 'the music of my people'
summary: Promise at sixteen to be a concert pianist, then Army and Juilliard led him to play Ellington, Waller and Henderson as his own culture's music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Did you have aspirations to become a professional classical pianist?

Yes. And at some point I did. When I was sixteen years old I made a promise to myself to become a concert pianist. I didn’t know that I was going to go to the Korean War. I didn’t know I was going to get in the Army. That kind of changed things. And then when I came out of the Army I went to Juilliard. And the time I spent in Juilliard let me know that it wasn’t the music of Chopin and Brahms and Beethoven that I had to play, it was the music of my people. I had to play Duke Ellington and Fats Waller and Fletcher Henderson. These are my people. Just as Rubenstein was playing the music of his people, Chopin. Just as Horowitz plays the music of his people, Scriabin and Rachmaninoff. I had to play the music of my people you see. And I think it’s not so much that you are forced to do that but it’s incumbent upon you. You are born into a certain situation. And you have to learn to accept that and to do something with that. Because world culture can only become a blend if people accept it and understand it. When people try to deny their particular culture, well then what they do is they eliminate something. They eliminate something of humanity. But when people recognize the individual culture of their people, where they come from, then they contribute to world humanity. That’s so much more important to me than nationalism or just this thing belongs here. No, we’re on a planet. We’re on a place where everybody is involved. That’s the thing that’s so beautiful about it is that there’s so many differences and we all have to contribute to it. And so that was

like an awakening to me. I like to call it an epiphany because when I was young, nobody ever talked to me about that kind of stuff. And then I became aware of all of these great people. I mean Willie “The Lion” Smith was a great pianist, Lucky Roberts was a great pianist, Scott Joplin was a great composer, Jelly Roll Morton was a great composer. These people, they meant something. And all of that now, a hundred years later, is meaning something to everybody in the United States. Young people who don’t get that information, it may take them until they’re 65 or 70 years old to understand where they come from. But I was lucky to get that before I was 30 years old and to know that this is the direction I have to go in, and not so much playing Chopin etudes, even though I use all of that all the time.
Right. Was it a gradual realization for you?

I think it was a kind of — I can’t say it was gradual because after I came out of the Army it seemed to me that that’s what I had to do. And when I went to Juilliard I concentrated on developing piano skills for that reason, not necessarily to play concert. Although at the age of sixteen I said that’s what I want to do, I want to be a concert pianist. But coming out of Juilliard I said well if I am going to be a concert pianist, it’s going to be in a different way. It’s certainly going to be playing “Daydreams,” or “Lush Life” or something like that.
